fields.name: demonstration
fields.description: At the video cycle, write all supplied V frame labels in chronological order, including the last frame. At every act cycle copy the incoming list unchanged; do not replace demonstration images with execution images. If no demonstration has yet been supplied, write an empty list. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V112", "V128", "V144", "V160", "V176", "V192", "V208", "V222"]
fields.annotation: The ordered list of every frame label supplied in the video cycle, including the last frame. This preserves the demonstrated manipulation: which peg was selected, where along that peg it was grasped, and the approach and insertion geometry. Write the list at the video cycle and carry it unchanged through every act cycle. Before a video has been supplied the value is an empty list. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V112", "V128", "V144", "V160", "V176", "V192", "V208", "V222"]

action:
At a video cycle output memory only. Execution starts with the open hand above the scene. Read demonstration to identify the peg actually lifted, the particular colored end between the fingers, and the box face entered by the other end. Track the selected peg backward to its initial position; do not select by color alone, since multiple pegs can share colors. Distinguish grasping an end from inserting that end: the free end enters the box. The selected box face can be on either image side. Robot left is +y, which appears on the right of the front image.

Use calibrated image geometry rather than copying episode-specific world coordinates. Recover tabletop peg axes and endpoints by intersecting camera rays with their appropriate height planes. Fit the box footprint and orientation from its edges. Use the wrist image to refine visible geometry. Determine peg identity, grasped end, and contact position separately. Use closing and early lifting demonstration frames together to identify the segment actually between the fingertips; the prominently projecting segment may be the free end. Trace the grasped segment back to the unobstructed initial peg. Fit its endpoints and color boundary in the current calibrated views and recover the demonstrated contact position along that segment, rather than using the peg midpoint. At pickup use a downward hand, roll approximately -pi and pitch approximately zero, align the hand's longitudinal axis with the peg, and close across its width; choose the yaw equivalent that matches the demonstration. For later manipulation, reconstruct the demonstrated orientation rather than imposing zero pitch.

Apply the following rules according to the observed pose, held object, and motion frames, not according to cycle number. If the hand is empty and not yet above the demonstrated grasp location, move open to that location at z=0.20 m with the pickup yaw. If it is open above that location near z=0.20 m, descend to the same nominal x,y at z=0.01 m and close. Recompute the nominal contact location from the visible peg geometry at the elevated open-hand configuration, not from the reached TCP. Use this same nominal x,y for the open approach, closing descent, and pickup lift. A reached approach displaced by more than a centimetre does not imply that the intended approach and contact locations differ. If the fingers have closed around the selected peg near table height, lift closed to z=0.20 m at that same nominal location and yaw.

If the selected peg has been lifted but has not yet been transported to the insertion approach, move closed to the demonstrated elevated transport endpoint. Identify this endpoint by completed lateral relocation and rotation before descent, and reconstruct it separately from the low staging pose before inward entry. Fit each pose relative to the entered box face using neighboring demonstration frames, visible peg endpoints, color boundary, and fingertip geometry. Recover the TCP-to-peg offset and constrain the actual held-peg offset with the current wrist image. If the hand is partly outside the image, infer its position from the visible held peg and demonstrated grasp offset, not an arbitrary clearance beyond the face. Project elevated geometry at its elevated height, not onto the tabletop. The TCP is neither the free tip nor the opening center. Resolve yaw's pi ambiguity using the directed vector from the held end to the free end. Reproduce demonstrated transport tilt and height; approximately 0.19 m is only an initial estimate for nearly level transport, not a universal target. Do not assume the transport endpoint lies directly above low staging, and do not move directly from pickup into the opening.

If the hand is at the elevated transport endpoint, move closed to the independently reconstructed low staging pose immediately before inward entry. Compute its intended box-relative position rather than preserving the measured transport endpoint. Ordinary transport tracking error is not evidence of a demonstrated inward translation during descent; include such translation only when the demonstrated geometry supports it. Reconstruct height and pitch together so the free tip approaches the opening correctly. For nearly level staging, TCP height near 0.04 m is an initial estimate, not an invariant; preserve demonstrated lower or tilted staging when present. If the hand is at low staging, target the next demonstrated opening-entry configuration. Entry may combine inward translation with height and pitch correction rather than remaining horizontal at constant height. Align the free tip with the opening, not the TCP.

After an inward advance, compare the current motion frames and free-tip-to-opening relationship with the ordered demonstration configurations. Distinguish low staging, intermediate opening entry, and terminal insertion; completing one advance does not automatically select the terminal pose. If the free tip remains outside and a demonstrated intermediate entry configuration remains, target that configuration before terminal insertion. Reconstruct each target's position, height, and orientation from its demonstrated geometry rather than imposing a fixed advance length or a universal 0.05 m cap. When terminal insertion is the next appropriate configuration, use the final demonstration frames, current box geometry, actual grasp offset, and remaining exposed peg length to reconstruct the final TCP position outside the entered face. Do not place the TCP at the opening or infer insertion depth from the free tip alone. Keep the gripper closed through the demonstrated pickup lift, transport, staging, and insertion motions. A red indicator confirms successful insertion but specifies neither an additional waypoint nor a gripper command. Apply any separately supplied post-success action convention; do not extrapolate an unseen continuation from the terminal demonstration image.

Use the current motion frames to distinguish a completed lift from completed transport and a completed descent from completed horizontal insertion. Compare the current configuration to the retained demonstration when the current wrist view shows only the held peg or table; do not interpret an occluded box as a missing box. Allow approximately centimetre-scale tracking error when recognizing a completed long move, but compute the next waypoint from the intended geometry.

For an unlisted or uncertain configuration, localize the held peg, box, and closest demonstrated configuration again. If holding the peg with uncertain clearance, lift vertically to safe clearance before correcting alignment; if empty, approach the demonstrated peg open. Never insert blindly when the free tip is visibly misaligned. Use a small corrective waypoint when necessary, and never issue an identical TCP waypoint merely to change the gripper. No purposeless waiting is required.
